A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same exploratory causal inference study and NES algorithm. Their full text, equations, figures, tables and appendices are readable, and retained material can be matched reliably across the expanded revision.

before.justification: V1 reports original CelebA-based simulated trials, comparative experiments and ablations, together with the authors' analysis of the ISTAnt ecological trial.

after.justification: V2 retains those empirical results and adds representation diagnostics, robustness experiments, additional baseline comparisons and further quantitative analysis of ISTAnt.

M1.justification: The foundation-model/SAE pipeline and recursive NES selection and stratification procedure are retained. V2 explicitly marks residualization as optional, but v1 Appendix A.3 already documented that option. Alternative encoders and activations are evaluated as ablations.

E1.justification: CelebA, its selected attributes, and ISTAnt remain unchanged. Appendix E.2.3 adds a limited simulation scenario with unequal outcome effects, testing recovery of weaker effects alongside stronger ones. Despite the heading 'Opposite effects,' the specified grid contains positive effects with differing magnitudes, not opposite signs.

E2.justification: V1 compares NES with Bonferroni, FDR, uncorrected t-tests and top-k selection. V2 retains these and evaluates sparse logistic regression and stability-selected LASSO, displayed as CFL (Lasso) and CFL (Lasso+) in Figure 37. This substantially broadens comparison to multivariate treatment-prediction methods.

E3.justification: V2 introduces controlled evaluations across foundation models, SAE widths from 3,072 to 12,288, top-k activation settings and JumpReLU, and residualization choices. It also tests treatment-assignment probabilities of 0.2, 0.4, 0.6 and 0.8 at specified sample sizes. These extend the experimental design while retaining the original dataset splits and evaluation metrics.

E4.justification: V1's alignment checks, null-effect test, testing-rule ablation and AD/AIPW comparison are retained. V2 adds foundation-model probes, encoder-width and sparsity sensitivity, separate SAE-seed replications, a JumpReLU failure analysis, residualization comparisons, and unequal-effect and treatment-imbalance stress tests. Appendix E substantially expands examination of why and when NES works.

E5.justification: V1 describes ten seeds combining trial redraws and SAE initializations. V2 specifies ten trial resamples per trained representation and reporting of mean plus or minus standard deviation, with two additional SAE initializations reported separately. This changes the description and attribution of variability; it does not establish an increased run count for the retained plots.

E6.justification: The original main benchmark plot is retained as Figure 5, and grooming F1 remains 0.398. V2 adds substantial condition-specific results for representation quality, robustness and new baselines, including near-zero NES precision with JumpReLU in Figure 24. It also newly reports background-code F1 of 0.568. These are added outcomes, not improvements to the retained main scores.

T1.justification: Section 2 replaces independence of T and W given Y and minimal I(Y;X) with a minimal sufficient (Y,W) representation satisfying independence of T and X given (Y,W). Appendix A.3 adds asymptotic FWER/FDR and O(n^-1/2) detectability remarks. The principal NES assumptions, theorems and proofs remain substantially unchanged.

C1.justification: The abstract is unchanged. The central contributions remain exploratory treatment-effect discovery through foundation models and SAEs, the significance-collapse paradox, NES recovery, and validation on simulated and ecological trials. The expanded experiments support these retained claims.

C2.justification: V2 develops concrete applicability limits: representation assumptions cannot be checked without outcome supervision, DINOv2 has weaker hat alignment, and JumpReLU can invalidate principal-neuron ground truth. It also revises the interpretation of the unchanged testing-rule curves, recognizing similar high-power performance rather than v1's claimed exact stopping advantage, and qualifies the ecological neurons' semantic interpretations.

D1.justification: V2 documents additional configuration grids and the stability-selection threshold of 0.6. Its reproducibility statement removes v1's submitted-code assertion and planned standalone-code release while retaining the Python snippet. A new inconsistency limits reproducibility: Table 1 specifies top-k = 5, whereas Appendix E describes 20 as the main setting.

R1.justification: V2 adds Cremer et al. (2007) for the social-immunity motivation and develops the connection to previously cited Causal Feature Learning through the new heuristic baselines. The main related-work positioning is retained. The renamed Cadei et al. (2025) reference identifies the same preprint.

P1.justification: Appendix E is substantially reorganized around assumption validation, method consistency and additional baselines, redistributing v1's separate full-results and ablation sections. V2 adds an appendix contents page and rewrites substantial motivating, problem-formulation and interpretation passages. This structural revision extends beyond simply appending experiments.

P2.justification: V2 updates the pipeline illustration, adds a boxed motivating example and a recursive NES diagram, and introduces numerous representation galleries and experimental panels. Existing benchmark, ecological, testing-rule and AIPW graphics are largely reused and relocated, with revised numbering and captions; the training tables are retained.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially addresses the limited testing of representation dependence in v1 through encoder, sparsity, width and residualization studies, additional multivariate comparators, and a concrete JumpReLU failure case. These additions make the central assumptions and applicability limits much more assessable. Correcting the interpretation of retained testing-rule curves also improves accuracy. These gains outweigh the limited reproducibility setbacks from conflicting top-k settings and removed code-release statements; they do not establish stronger main performance or resolve the largely unchanged theoretical arguments.
